title: The Balance Sheet Equation
context: Analyze how the balance sheet equation requires total assets to equal the sum of total liabilities and total equity. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A pallet loader used by an operating business is classified as inventory because inventory can include any physical equipment a business owns.
A pallet loader held by a dealer for resale to customers is classified as a non-current asset because the dealer is a business rather than a household.
A pallet loader kept in service by an operating business for more than one year is classified as a non-current tangible asset.
The same pallet loader must always be classified identically on every balance sheet regardless of how it is held.
The same pallet loader may be a non-current asset for one business and inventory for another, depending on whether it is used or held for sale.
tactical_explanations:
Physical form alone does not make a pallet loader inventory. Inventory is held for sale or for cycle consumption — not every machine the firm owns. Operating use beyond a year puts pallet loader among non-current tangibles. Counterexample: a forklift in the firm’s own warehouse is plant, not stock.

So the statement is False.

A dealer’s pallet loader held for customers is merchandise.

So the statement is False.

Multi-year operating use of a pallet loader fits the non-current tangible test. Useful life beyond the period plus own use — not resale — drive that line. Tangible means physical substance; non-current means long-term benefit.

So the statement is True.

The same pallet loader need not share one balance-sheet line everywhere. Each reporter classifies by how it holds the object. Operator → non-current tangible; dealer → inventory. Physical identity does not freeze the category.

So the statement is False.

Intended use decides the line for the same physical object.

So the statement is True.

title: Assets Equal Liabilities Plus Equity
context: Review how owner's equity is derived as the residual claim remaining once liabilities are deducted from assets. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Classifying a pallet loader as a non-current asset depends mainly on its purchase price rather than on management's intended use.
Classifying a pallet loader as a non-current asset depends on management's intention to use it in operations rather than to sell it quickly.
A pallet loader acquired for resale still counts among non-current assets as long as it remains unsold for several months.
A pallet loader used daily in a business's own operations should be recorded as inventory because it wears out over time.
Once a dealer sells a pallet loader from its stock, the buyer must continue to record it as inventory.
tactical_explanations:
Purchase price measures cost; it does not choose inventory vs fixed asset. Management intent — operate or resell — decides the class. A cheap pallet loader used for years is still non-current; a costly one held for sale is inventory.

So the statement is False.

Intent to use the asset in operations beyond one period places it among non-current assets.

So the statement is True.

Goods bought for resale enter inventory immediately. Sitting unsold for months does not promote them into non-current assets. Resale intent, not shelf time, decides the line.

So the statement is False.

Wear is handled by depreciating a fixed asset, not by calling operating kit inventory. Daily own use of a pallet loader supports non-current classification. Counterexample: factory machines wear out yet sit in plant & equipment.

So the statement is False.

After the sale, the buyer’s purpose governs classification.

So the statement is False.

title: Owner's Equity as a Residual Claim
context: Analyze the distinction drawn between non-current assets and current assets based on expected holding period. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: When a pallet loader is acquired to be resold rather than used, it belongs among current assets as inventory.
A pallet loader bought by a business to support its own daily operations is a tangible fixed asset because it delivers benefit across several accounting periods.
A pallet loader that a dealer displays for sale is not a fixed asset of that dealer.
An industrial dishwasher kept in service by an operating business for more than one year is classified as a non-current tangible asset.
An industrial dishwasher held by a dealer for resale to customers is classified as inventory, a current asset, rather than a non-current asset.
tactical_explanations:
Bought to resell, a pallet loader belongs in inventory (current).

So the statement is True.

A pallet loader bought for the firm’s own daily work is a tangible fixed asset. Benefit spans periods; it is not held for sale. Tangible fixed assets sit among non-current assets on the sheet.

So the statement is True.

A dealer displaying a pallet loader for sale holds inventory. That stock is not the dealer’s fixed asset.

So the statement is True.

Multi-year operating use of an industrial dishwasher fits the non-current tangible test.

So the statement is True.

Dealer stock of an industrial dishwasher is inventory — a current asset. It is not the dealer’s non-current operating asset. Held for sale beats physical durability when choosing the line.

So the statement is True.

title: Non-Current Versus Current Assets
context: Review why non-current assets are expected to deliver benefit to a business for more than one year. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: The same industrial dishwasher may be a non-current asset for one business and inventory for another, depending on whether it is used or held for sale.
An industrial dishwasher used by an operating business is classified as inventory because inventory can include any physical equipment a business owns.
An industrial dishwasher held by a dealer for resale to customers is classified as a non-current asset because the dealer is a business rather than a household.
The same industrial dishwasher must always be classified identically on every balance sheet regardless of how it is held.
Classifying an industrial dishwasher as a non-current asset depends on management's intention to use it in operations rather than to sell it quickly.
tactical_explanations:
Intended use decides the line for the same physical object. An operator records a non-current tangible; a dealer records inventory. That dual outcome is exactly what use-versus-resale predicts.

So the statement is True.

Physical form alone does not make an industrial dishwasher inventory. Inventory is held for sale or for cycle consumption — not every machine the firm owns. Operating use beyond a year puts industrial dishwasher among non-current tangibles. Counterexample: a forklift in the firm’s own warehouse is plant, not stock.

So the statement is False.

A dealer’s industrial dishwasher held for customers is merchandise.

So the statement is False.

The same industrial dishwasher need not share one balance-sheet line everywhere. Each reporter classifies by how it holds the object. Operator → non-current tangible; dealer → inventory. Physical identity does not freeze the category.

So the statement is False.

Intent to use the asset in operations beyond one period places it among non-current assets. Resale intent would have put the same object in inventory.

So the statement is True.

Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: Non-current assets normally have a useful life of more than one year and are intended to be used in the business for longer than one year.
Non-current liabilities amount to less than 56.8% of total equity in Year 2.
The combined total of equity and non-current liabilities exceeds non-current assets by more than 7.3% in Year 1.
Total equity grew by more than 24.5% between Year 1 and Year 2.
Total assets grew by more than 10% between Year 1 and Year 2.
tactical_explanations:
Non-current assets are held for use beyond one accounting period. Useful life beyond a year plus operating intent define the category.

So the statement is True.

NCL-to-equity share = non-current liabilities ÷ total equity.

$$
\text{NCL share} = \frac{\text{non-current liabilities}}{\text{total equity}}
$$

Non-current liabilities combine the long-term loan and bonds lines: From the extract: Equity = 839.

$$
\text{NCL} = 220 + 63 = 283
$$

$$
\frac{283}{839} \approx 0.3373 \approx 33.7\%
$$

Year 2 NCL/equity is 33.7%, so it is less than 56.8%.

So the statement is True.

Long-term financing surplus = (equity + non-current liabilities) ÷ non-current assets − 1.

$$
\text{Surplus} = \frac{\text{equity} + \text{NCL}}{\text{NCA}} - 1
$$

From the extract: NCA = 740.

$$
\text{Equity} + \text{NCL} = 761 + 267 = 1{,}028
$$

$$
\frac{1{,}028}{740} \approx 1.3892
$$

$$
\frac{1{,}028}{740} - 1 \approx 0.3892 \approx 38.9\%
$$

The surplus is 38.9%, which exceeds 7.3%.

So the statement is True.

Percentage growth for Total equity is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1.

$$
\text{growth} = \frac{\text{Year 2} - \text{Year 1}}{\text{Year 1}}
$$

From the extract: Year 1 = 761, Year 2 = 839.

$$
\text{Year 2} - \text{Year 1} = 839 - 761 = 78
$$

$$
\frac{78}{761} \approx 0.1025 \approx 10.2\%
$$

The claim says growth of more than 24.5%. Actual growth is 10.2%, which is not more than the claimed 24.5%.

So the statement is False.

Percentage growth for Total assets is (Year 2 − Year 1) ÷ Year 1.

$$
\text{growth} = \frac{\text{Year 2} - \text{Year 1}}{\text{Year 1}}
$$

From the extract: Year 1 = 1,181, Year 2 = 1,279.

$$
\text{Year 2} - \text{Year 1} = 1{,}279 - 1{,}181 = 98
$$

$$
\frac{98}{1{,}181} \approx 0.0830 \approx 8.3\%
$$

The claim says growth of more than 10%. Actual growth is 8.3%, which is not more than the claimed 10%.

So the statement is False.

title: Raising Equity Versus Taking on Debt
context: Analyze how a vehicle can be a fixed asset for one business and inventory for a dealer. Evaluate the following economic assertions:
statements: A development patent is recorded as an intangible non-current asset alongside tangible assets such as buildings and machinery.
An espresso machine acquired for resale still counts among non-current assets as long as it remains unsold for several months.
An espresso machine used daily in a business's own operations should be recorded as inventory because it wears out over time.
Once a dealer sells an espresso machine from its stock, the buyer must continue to record it as inventory.
A printing press used by an operating business is classified as inventory because inventory can include any physical equipment a business owns.
tactical_explanations:
Classification for development patent follows use, benefit timing, and settlement timing.

So the statement is True.

Goods bought for resale enter inventory immediately. Sitting unsold for months does not promote them into non-current assets. Resale intent, not shelf time, decides the line.

So the statement is False.

Wear is handled by depreciating a fixed asset, not by calling operating kit inventory.

So the statement is False.

After the sale, the buyer’s purpose governs classification. If the buyer puts the machine into operations, it becomes the buyer’s non-current asset. The seller’s old inventory label does not travel with the object forever.

So the statement is False.

Physical form alone does not make a printing press inventory. Inventory is held for sale or for cycle consumption — not every machine the firm owns. Operating use beyond a year puts printing press among non-current tangibles. Counterexample: a forklift in the firm’s own warehouse is plant, not stock.

So the statement is False.
